intro: German is a pluricentric language: Germany, Austria and Switzerland each have their own standard variety, and Austrian and Swiss Standard German are no less correct than the German spoken in Hamburg — they are not dialects. They differ above all in vocabulary: Austria says Jänner, Paradeiser, Erdäpfel, Marillen, Topfen, Obers, Matura, Trafik and heuer; Switzerland says Velo, parkieren, grillieren, Trottoir, Billett, Znüni, Estrich (attic) and allenfalls (if necessary); both say Spital. There are also a few grammar differences, such as the perfect with sein (ich bin gesessen), and Swiss spelling never uses ß. The goal is to read Austrian and Swiss newspapers, official letters and recipes without stumbling. In this quiz the German line tells you the region and the word used in Germany; type the Austrian or Swiss standard word — or, in the two items marked with an arrow, the German-German equivalent.
tips[0].title: Austria: the kitchen and the calendar
tips[0].text: Jänner (Januar), Paradeiser (Tomaten), Erdäpfel (Kartoffeln), Marillen (Aprikosen), Topfen (Quark), Obers / Schlagobers (Sahne), Karfiol (Blumenkohl), Kren (Meerrettich), Sessel (Stuhl), Matura (Abitur), Trafik (Tabak- und Zeitschriftenladen), heuer (dieses Jahr). When Austria joined the EU in 1995, a protocol gave 23 Austrian food terms — among them Erdäpfel, Marillen, Topfen, Paradeiser and Obers — equal legal standing with their German-German counterparts.
tips[0].trap: Sessel in Austria is an ordinary chair; the upholstered armchair is a Fauteuil.
tips[0].check.why: Marille is the Austrian apricot; Paradeiser is a tomato and Topfen is quark.
tips[1].title: Switzerland: French loans and -ieren
tips[1].text: Swiss Standard German borrows from French and likes the ending -ieren: Velo (Fahrrad), Trottoir (Gehweg), Billett (Fahrkarte), Poulet (Hähnchen), Glace (Eis), parkieren (parken), grillieren (grillen). Everyday life has its own words: Znüni (mid-morning snack), Estrich (Dachboden), Gesuch (Antrag), Busse (Geldstrafe), allenfalls (gegebenenfalls), Matur or Matura (Abitur). Spital (Krankenhaus) is standard in both Switzerland and Austria.
tips[1].trap: Estrich in Germany is floor screed; in Switzerland it is the attic. allenfalls in Germany means at most, in Switzerland if necessary.
tips[1].check.why: Velo is the Swiss standard word for bicycle; Billett is a ticket and Trottoir the pavement.
tips[2].title: Grammar and spelling
tips[2].text: In Austria, Switzerland and southern Germany sitzen, stehen and liegen form the perfect with sein: Ich bin gesessen, Das Auto ist vor dem Haus gestanden, Er ist im Bett gelegen. Swiss Standard German writes ss wherever Germany and Austria write ß: Strasse, Grüsse, schliesslich, gross. Some genders differ too: in Austria das Cola and das E-Mail are common, and in Switzerland das Tram.
tips[2].check.why: Swiss Standard German never uses ß and writes ss instead.
tips[3].title: Standard, not dialect
tips[3].text: Everything in this quiz is written standard language: it appears in newspapers, laws, school books and official letters in Austria or Switzerland. Dialect is something else — Swiss German dialects (Schweizerdeutsch) and Austrian dialects are spoken varieties you are not expected to write. So Velo and Jänner belong in a formal written text; dialect spellings do not.
tips[3].check.why: Billett is written standard in Switzerland; the dialect forms lösed, de and es belong to spoken Swiss German, not to formal writing.

hook: Read a Viennese menu or a Zurich notice without stumbling: Marillen, Jänner, Velo and Billett are standard German too.
